div: The Batch Decay tool decays many initial nuclides at once — either to a single future (or past) time, or across a number of evenly spaced time steps — and presents the results as a table you can export to CSV or copy to the clipboard.

Entering nuclides. Add a row for each initial nuclide with the + button, or drag and drop (or click to upload) a CSV onto the drop area to replace all rows at once. A CSV in one of the formats below can also be dropped onto the main InterSpec window (or opened with InterSpec) while this tool is closed, which opens the tool with the file loaded. Each row takes a nuclide, an optional initial age (enabled only for nuclides whose result depends on age), and an initial activity. The - button removes a row.

Activity units. The activity accepts a value with a unit of either becquerel or curie, with an optional metric prefix — for example bq, kBq, MBq, GBq, TBq, mBq, uBq, or Ci, mCi, uCi, nCi, pCi, fCi (unit text is not case sensitive). You may instead enter a bare number with no unit, which is interpreted as becquerel. Because all rows share a single units style, a bare number is only kept as becquerel when every row is a bare number; if any row specifies a unit, the bare numbers are given that same unit.

CSV input. Three formats are accepted. A simple format with one nuclide,activity pair per line (a bare activity number is interpreted as becquerel; blank lines and lines beginning with # are ignored). A header-keyed format with Product, Value, and Unit columns; any areal/volumetric suffix on the unit (for example /m2) is carried through to the output labels. Or the multi-location format described next.

Multiple locations. If the CSV's first column names a physical location (for example a probe or sample name), each location is treated as its own independent set of inputs. Its nuclides appear together in the input area under the location's name, the nuclides of a location are co-decayed as a single mixture, and the output carries one block of rows per location, with any extra columns (such as latitude and longitude) echoed through. Activities from different locations are never mixed or summed.

Location names that differ only by a trailing index — Probe-01_1, Probe-01_2, … — are read as the one location Probe-01, since tools that write these files often number each nuclide's row separately. A name is only shortened this way when the result stays unambiguous; if it would merge two locations that hold the same nuclide, or that disagree on their other columns, the full names are kept instead. A file whose locations hold a single nuclide each carries no grouping information, and is read as one ungrouped set.
Removing every nuclide from a location removes that group. There is no way to create a group by hand: grouping only ever comes from a file that names locations.

Options. Choose the decay time and number of steps, an optional minimum activity, the activity units (Becquerel or Curie), whether to sum all inputs into a single co-decaying mixture (Mix inputs), whether to also report every decay progeny (Show progeny), and which quantities to include (activity, x-rays, gammas, alphas, betas). While a multi-location file is loaded, Mix inputs is fixed on and disabled, since each location is always co-decayed and locations are never combined.

Minimum activity. An optional lower cut on the results: any activity below it is left out. It is a plain number with no units, compared against the value as shown in the result table, so it is in whatever activity units the results are in. A location whose every row falls below the cut drops out of the output entirely. When several time steps are shown, a row is dropped only if it is below the cut at every step, so the table stays rectangular. The gamma, x-ray, alpha and beta line rows are counts per second rather than activities, so the cut does not apply to them.

Decaying backwards. A negative decay time (for example -48h) solves for the activities the inputs must have had that long ago, given what they are now. Inputs that are decayed together — with Mix inputs on, or the nuclides of one location in a multi-location file — and that share an ancestor are coupled, so this is not simply a division per nuclide: for example the past Cs137 partly accounts for the Ba137m measured today. With Mix inputs off each input is solved on its own. Two consequences are worth knowing:

A short-lived nuclide's own past activity may be unrecoverable. If essentially none of what was there then survives to now — 48 hours is over a thousand Ba137m half-lives — then nothing measurable today constrains it. When one of its parents is among the inputs, it is reported as zero and its present activity is attributed to ingrowth from them. When no parent is, there is nothing to attribute it to and no meaningful number to report, so the calculation stops with a message naming the nuclide; shorten the time until it is within reach. Either way this is a genuine limit of the measurement, not an approximation.

The inputs may be mutually inconsistent. A parent and progeny measured today imply a past state; if no past state can reproduce both, the tool reports the discrepancy as a warning naming the nuclide, the value measured, the value its ancestors imply, and the percent difference, rather than silently returning a set that does not decay back to the input.

An initial age is the age of the sample when it was measured, i.e. at time zero of the results. Looking back, the sample was correspondingly younger; if the age is shorter than how far back you look, the sample is taken as freshly made at that past time, and a note says so.

Mix inputs. With this on, all inputs are placed into a single mixture and co-decayed, so the decay progeny of different ultimate parents mix together and are reported as a single line per nuclide. With it off, each input is decayed on its own; a progeny reached from more than one input is then reported separately for each parent (its activity line notes which input it came from). Gammas and x-rays are always reported for progeny; each line notes the parent -> child transition that emits it.
The tool's state can be captured as a link or QR code from the window footer, participates in undo/redo, and is saved with (and restored from) the application state.
